title: Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion
short: Energy swaps between ½kx² and ½mv², and the total is ½kA².
trouble: Students think the speed is greatest at the turning points.

blocks.html: An oscillator trades energy back and forth between motion and storage. Conservation of mechanical energy turns that trade into quick answers about speeds, without any graphs or timing, for any simple harmonic oscillator.

A spring stretched by $x$ stores $U = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$. With no friction, the total $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ never changes. At a turning point the mass stops for an instant, so all the energy is stored: $E = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$. At equilibrium the spring stores nothing, so all of it is kinetic: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$. In between, the energy is shared.

$$\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2.$$ The speed is greatest at equilibrium, $v_{\max} = A\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$, and zero at the turning points. At any position, $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}\left(A^2 - x^2\right)}$.

blocks.name: ph-energy

opts.task: Drag the point along the bowl. The gap between the total-energy line and the curve is the kinetic energy.

blocks.cap: The spring's energy $U = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ is a bowl. The total energy is a flat line; where they meet are the turning points, and the gap between them is $K$.

blocks.title: Total energy and top speed
blocks.q: A $0.50\ \text{kg}$ block on a spring ($k = 50\ \text{N/m}$) oscillates with amplitude $0.10\ \text{m}$. Find its total energy and greatest speed.

blocks.title: Speed partway
blocks.q: For the same block, how fast is it moving at $x = 0.06\ \text{m}$?

blocks.title: Where the energy splits evenly
steps: Then $U$ is half the total: $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$, so $x = \dfrac{A}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.71A$.
For $A = 0.10\ \text{m}$ that is $0.071\ \text{m}$, not halfway, because $U$ grows as $x^2$.

blocks.html: Thinking the speed is greatest at the turning points. The turning points are where the mass stops and reverses, so the speed there is zero; what is greatest there is the stored energy (and the acceleration). The speed peaks at equilibrium, where all the energy is kinetic. Check with energy: at $x = \pm A$ the spring already holds the whole $\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$, so nothing is left for motion.
